chunks: "Minimum useful UART is three wires: TX, RX and ground. TX carries data from device A to device B, RX carries data the other way, so you get full duplex.
Ground is the shared reference, because the logic levels are voltages measured against it, so I always count it even though it isn't a signal.
If you only need one direction, say a GPS module that just streams data to the MCU, you can get away with two wires: the module's TX to the MCU's RX, plus ground.
In real designs you'll sometimes see five: add RTS and CTS for hardware flow control, so that a module with a small buffer can tell the host to pause.
A full RS-232 port uses nine pins, but most of those are modem-control legacy.
And if it goes over RS-485, the two data lines become a differential pair, so you've got A and B for half-duplex, or two pairs for full duplex, plus a ground reference or shield.
Compare that with SPI, where you need four wires plus one extra chip select per device, or I2C, where two wires are shared by the whole bus."
